places.name: Grand Palace & Wat Phra Kaew
places.line: Gold spires, the Emerald Buddha and Bangkok's most famous sight.
places.about: The former royal residence and its temple of the Emerald Buddha form a walled city of glittering spires, murals and guardian giants. It is busy and hot, and worth it.
tips: Go at opening time to beat the heat and the tour groups.
Strict dress code: shoulders and knees covered, no see-through clothes. Wraps can be rented nearby.
Ignore anyone outside who says it's closed today: it's a classic scam.

Best photographed from the east bank at sunset.
Shoulders and knees covered inside the grounds.

places.line: Bangkok's night-time food street: noodles, seafood and smoke.

tips: Arrive around 7 pm when most stalls are open.
Follow the longest local queues.
Closed on some Mondays; check before you go.

places.name: Ayutthaya
places.line: Ruined capital of old Siam, an easy day trip from Bangkok.
places.about: Ayutthaya was the kingdom's capital for four centuries until it was sacked in 1767. Brick towers, headless Buddhas and the famous Buddha head in tree roots are spread across a riverside island.
tips: Rent a bicycle or a tuk-tuk for the day: the sites are spread out.
Trains from Bangkok take about 1.5 to 2 hours and cost very little.
Never pose above the Buddha head in the roots: it's disrespectful.

places.name: Erawan Falls, Kanchanaburi
places.line: Seven tiers of turquoise pools in the forest.
places.about: In Erawan National Park, a stream drops through seven limestone tiers into milky turquoise pools you can swim in. Kanchanaburi town, with the Bridge on the River Kwai, makes a good base.
tips: Start early and walk up to the top tiers before the crowds.
Bring swimwear and water shoes; the small fish nibble.
National park entry fee applies, higher for foreigners.

places.name: Sukhothai Historical Park
places.line: Calm, green ruins of the first Thai kingdom.
places.about: Lotus ponds, seated Buddhas and lotus-bud towers from the 13th century, spread through a quiet park. Quieter and more serene than Ayutthaya.
tips: Cycle the park at sunrise or late afternoon.
Stay in New Sukhothai or near the park gate.
Loy Krathong (November) is especially beautiful here.

places.name: Chiang Mai Old City
places.line: A walled, walkable old town full of temples and cafés.
places.about: Inside the moat of Chiang Mai sit dozens of temples, from the ruined great chedi of Wat Chedi Luang to teak halls, along with cafés, massage schools and the Sunday Walking Street market.
tips: Sunday Walking Street market on Ratchadamnoen Road.
Grab and Bolt work well; red songthaews are shared taxis.
March and April can be smoky from seasonal burning.

places.name: Wat Phra That Doi Suthep
places.line: Golden hilltop temple overlooking Chiang Mai.
places.about: Chiang Mai's most revered temple sits on the mountain above the city, reached by a long naga-lined staircase or a small funicular. On clear days the view stretches over the valley.
tips: Go early morning for clear views and fewer people.
Walk the stairs up and take the funicular down, or the reverse.
Combine with the Monk's Trail hike for the adventurous.

places.name: Pai
places.line: A laid-back mountain valley town in Mae Hong Son.
places.about: Rice fields, hot springs, waterfalls and Pai Canyon at sunset, with a relaxed town of night markets and guesthouses. The winding road from Chiang Mai is famous for its many curves.
tips: Take motion-sickness pills for the mountain road from Chiang Mai.
Only ride a scooter if you're experienced; the roads are steep.
Nights get cool from December to February: bring a layer.

places.name: Wat Rong Khun (White Temple)
places.line: A dazzling white, mirror-studded modern temple in Chiang Rai.
places.about: Designed by the Thai artist Chalermchai Kositpipat, the White Temple is a work of art in progress: white plaster and mirror glass, a bridge over reaching hands, and surprising modern murals inside.
tips: Arrive at opening time; it fills up fast.
Pair it with the Blue Temple and Baan Dam (Black House) the same day.
Photography isn't allowed inside the main hall.

places.name: Khao Sok & Cheow Lan Lake
places.line: Rainforest, limestone cliffs and floating bungalows on a jade lake.
places.about: One of the oldest rainforests in the world surrounds a vast lake of emerald water and karst islands. Sleep in a floating raft house, kayak at dawn, and listen for gibbons.
tips: Book a one or two-night lake tour with a floating bungalow.
Bring a dry bag and leech socks in the rainy season.
Halfway between Phuket, Krabi and Surat Thani: an easy add-on.

places.name: Railay
places.line: Cliff-backed beaches reachable only by boat.
places.about: Towering limestone walls cut Railay off from the mainland, so you arrive by longtail boat from Ao Nang or Krabi. Climbing, lagoons, and some of Thailand's most dramatic beaches, including Phra Nang.
tips: Longtail boats leave from Ao Nang beach when full.
Phra Nang beach in the early morning, before the day boats.
Rock climbing courses for complete beginners are easy to book.

places.name: Koh Phi Phi
places.line: The famous twin bays and turquoise lagoons of the Andaman.
places.about: Phi Phi Don's viewpoint looks down on two curving bays; around it are snorkelling spots, Pileh Lagoon and Maya Bay on Phi Phi Leh. Busy and lively, best enjoyed outside the day-trip rush.
tips: Stay overnight to see the bays without the day-trippers.
Maya Bay closes for part of each year to recover: check before you go.
Climb to the viewpoint at sunrise or sunset.

Try local Phuket dishes like mee hokkien.
The island's beaches are a 20 to 40 minute ride away.

places.about: Lanta has long sandy beaches on its west coast, an old wooden fishing town on the east, and a national park at the southern tip. Calmer than Phi Phi and good for a slower week.

places.about: Samui has busy Chaweng, quieter Lamai and Bophut's Fisherman's Village, plus waterfalls and the Big Buddha. Boat trips run to Ang Thong Marine Park's islands.

places.name: Koh Tao
places.line: Small island, clear water, and one of the world's cheapest places to learn to dive.
places.about: Koh Tao is all coves, granite boulders and coral reefs, with a famous viewpoint over the three linked islets of Koh Nang Yuan. Many people come for a few days and stay to take a diving course.
tips: Open Water diving courses take about 3 to 4 days.

places.name: Koh Chang
places.line: A big green jungle island with easy beaches and a stilted fishing pier.
places.about: Thailand's second largest island is mostly national park: steep rainforest, waterfalls and a string of beaches down the west coast. White Sand Beach is busy and easy, Lonely Beach is for backpackers, and the south end still feels like a fishing village. It is the gateway to Koh Kood and Koh Mak.
tips: Base on the west coast: White Sand for convenience, Klong Prao or Kai Bae for families, Lonely Beach for cheap beds and bars.
The hill roads are very steep with tight bends; skip the scooter unless you ride well and use songthaews instead.
Go to Bang Bao pier early for snorkel boats to the southern islands and leave by late afternoon before the tour crowd eats.

places.name: Koh Kood
places.line: Clear water, quiet bays and a waterfall you can jump into.
places.about: Koh Kood sits at the far end of Thailand's east coast, close to Cambodia. There are no big towns or nightlife, just coconut groves, glassy water, mangrove rivers and resorts spread along empty bays. Come to switch off.
tips: Book a room with pier pickup; there is no public transport and taxis are few.
Bring enough cash from the mainland: ATMs are few and can run dry on holiday weekends.
Many resorts and boats slow down or close from about June to September, so check before you book.

places.name: Koh Mak
places.line: A flat, slow little island made for bicycles and sandbars.
places.about: Koh Mak is small, flat and mostly coconut and rubber plantations, owned for generations by a few local families who keep it low-key. No jet skis, no big resorts, just bike paths, calm beaches and a sandbar island you can wade to at low tide.
tips: Rent a bicycle for the whole stay; the island is flat and the roads are quiet.
Time a visit to Koh Kham with low tide and bring water: there is little shade.
Use Koh Mak as the middle stop between Koh Chang and Koh Kood to break up the boat ride.

places.name: Koh Samet
places.line: The closest real island beach to Bangkok, with soft white sand.
places.about: Koh Samet is small, sandy and only a few hours from Bangkok, so it is a weekend favourite for Thais. The east coast has a chain of coves from lively Hat Sai Kaew to quiet bays further south; Ao Prao on the west side is the sunset spot. It also gets less rain than most of Thailand.
tips: Go on weekdays; Friday night to Sunday the island fills with Bangkok groups and prices jump.
Pay the national park fee at the Na Dan entry point and keep the ticket.

places.about: Pattaya is honest about what it is: a loud seaside city where Walking Street and the beer bars are a big part of the draw, and the adult nightlife is very visible. places.about: Hua Hin is where the Thai royal family has summered for a century, and it still feels more relaxed than most beach towns. Expect a long beach, a pretty wooden railway station, excellent night markets, and day trips to caves and palaces nearby.

Plan a weekend for the Cicada and Tamarind markets, which open Friday to Sunday evenings.

tips: Join a guided day tour or hire a driver; the best wildlife spotting is with someone who knows where to look.
Wild elephants have right of way: stop, keep your distance and never get out of the car.
Avoid Thai long weekends when the park road jams; weekdays are far quieter.

places.name: Lopburi

places.about: Lopburi is an old royal city with Khmer temples and a 17th century palace, but most people come for the macaques that run the old town. They climb over Phra Prang Sam Yot, cross the railway and steal anything shiny. It makes an easy stop on the train between Ayutthaya and the north.
tips: Take off sunglasses, hats and earrings and carry nothing in plastic bags: the monkeys grab them.
Do it as a half day: leave bags at the station's left luggage and walk; most sights are within 10 minutes.
From November to January, add a drive to the sunflower fields east of town.

Koh Yao Noi is conservative: cover up in the villages and keep alcohol to resorts and bars.

places.about: The Similans are a national park of granite islands far off the Andaman coast, with powder white beaches, turtles and coral. They open only from about mid October to mid May. Most people visit on a long speedboat day trip from Khao Lak, while divers go by liveaboard to reach Koh Bon, Koh Tachai and Richelieu Rock.

Bring coral-safe sunscreen or a rash guard; harmful sunscreens are banned in the park.

places.line: A misty valley town of Shan temples, at the far end of the mountain loop.
places.about: Mae Hong Son is a quiet mountain town near the Myanmar border, with Shan-style temples reflected in a small lake and fog in the valleys most cool-season mornings. Ride the loop from Chiang Mai through Pai to get here, and use it as a base for tea villages, bamboo bridges and sunrise over the mist.
tips: Do the loop over 5 to 7 days; the roads are long and full of curves, so do not rush them.
Be up before dawn at Pang Ung or Doi Kong Mu for the mist; bring a jacket, it gets cold.
Think twice about the long-neck Karen villages, which charge entry and can feel like a show; choose a community-run visit if you go.

places.name: Doi Inthanon
places.line: Thailand's highest peak: cloud forest, waterfalls, twin royal pagodas and a ridge-top trail.
places.about: The summit sits at 2,565 metres, about two hours south-west of Chiang Mai, and is often wrapped in mist and moss. Most visitors stop at the twin pagodas built for the late King and Queen, then walk the Kew Mae Pan ridge trail through grassland and rhododendrons. On the way up and down are big waterfalls, a royal project farm and Karen and Hmong villages.
tips: Bring a warm layer: the top can drop below 10°C on winter mornings while Chiang Mai is still warm.
Kew Mae Pan is open roughly November to May and needs a local guide, hired at the trailhead for about 200 baht per group.
Hire a driver or join a small tour; the road is steep and long for a scooter, and public songthaews only go part of the way.

places.name: Ethical elephant sanctuary
places.line: Spend a day watching rescued elephants roam, bathe and eat, with no riding and no shows.
places.about: Elephant Nature Park in the Mae Taeng valley, about an hour north of Chiang Mai, is the best known of the sanctuaries that let elephants simply be elephants. Many of its herd were rescued from logging, trekking and street begging. Visits are about feeding, walking alongside and watching from the viewing platforms, not touching on demand.
tips: A genuinely ethical place has no riding, no tricks or painting, no chains on display and limits on bathing or hands-on contact.
Be wary of camps that just swapped the word camp for sanctuary: if the elephants are made to perform for each group, walk away.

places.line: A cave temple under a limestone giant, birdsong and slow mountain mornings.
places.about: Chiang Dao is a small valley town about 90 minutes north of Chiang Mai, overlooked by Doi Luang Chiang Dao, one of Thailand's highest peaks. Its sacred cave runs deep into the mountain, with Buddha images lit by lantern. Most people come to slow down in garden guesthouses, walk to forest temples and watch the mist lift off the cliffs.
tips: The deeper cave chambers are unlit: hire a lantern guide at the entrance and bring a torch for your own feet.
The Doi Luang summit trek is a two-day climb with a local guide; it opens only in the cool season with a daily quota, so check with your guesthouse well ahead.

places.name: Golden Triangle
places.line: Stand where Thailand, Laos and Myanmar meet on the Mekong, with an excellent opium museum.
places.about: The Golden Triangle is the spot north of Chiang Saen where the Ruak River joins the Mekong and three countries face each other. Beyond the giant Buddha and souvenir stalls, the Hall of Opium tells the region's drug-trade history well. Nearby Chiang Saen is an ancient walled town scattered with brick temple ruins.
tips: Give the Hall of Opium at least two hours; it is closed on Mondays.
Mekong boats to the Lao market island usually need your passport and are mainly shopping stops; a short river ride for the view is enough.
Combine with Chiang Saen's old temples and return via Mae Sai for a full day from Chiang Rai.

Wat Phumin's murals of everyday life, including a couple whispering, are its icon, and the old town is easy to cycle. Beyond it lie the high road to Doi Phu Kha and the mountain salt wells of Bo Kluea.
tips: Rent a bicycle for the old town: Wat Phumin, the national museum and Wat Phra That Chang Kham are all within a few blocks.
For Doi Phu Kha and Bo Kluea, hire a car or join a local tour; the mountain road is steep and has few buses.

places.name: River Kwai and the Death Railway

places.about: Kanchanaburi's iron bridge over the Khwae Yai river is part of the Thailand to Burma railway built by Allied prisoners and Asian labourers in World War Two, at a huge cost in lives. A slow third-class train still runs along the line past wooden viaducts to Nam Tok. The war cemeteries and the Hellfire Pass memorial tell the story with quiet power.
tips: Take the morning train from the bridge to Nam Tok; sit on the left going out for the river views at the Tham Krasae viaduct.
Hellfire Pass is about 80 km north of town; the museum and cutting walk need two to three hours.
Dress respectfully at the cemeteries and memorials.

places.about: Chatuchak is one of the world's biggest markets, with around 15,000 stalls spread over 27 sections north of the centre. It sells everything from vintage denim to ceramics and pets, with coconut ice cream to keep you going. Across the road, Or Tor Kor is a spotless food market famous for perfect fruit, curries and sweets.

places.line: Limestone peaks, marshes and a cave with a royal pavilion lit by a beam of sunlight.
places.about: Khao Sam Roi Yot National Park, about an hour south of Hua Hin, is a coast of jagged limestone hills, mangroves and freshwater marsh full of birds. Its star is Phraya Nakhon Cave, where a golden pavilion sits in a collapsed cavern under a shaft of light. Reach it by boat or headland path, then a steep climb.

places.line: Forty-odd jungle islands in a turquoise sea, with a hidden emerald lake.

Big boats are cheaper and steadier; speedboats are faster and visit more spots.

places.about: Phanom Rung crowns an extinct volcano in Buriram, reached by a grand processional way with naga bridges, and its doors line up so the sun shines straight through all fifteen a few days a year. Nearby Prasat Muang Tam is a lower temple ringed by lotus ponds. Phimai, closer to Korat, is a beautifully restored sandstone temple at the heart of a small town.

places.line: Old wooden shophouses on the Mekong, sunrise over mist and a famous walking street.
places.about: Chiang Khan is a small Loei river town of teak shophouses facing Laos across the Mekong. It is a hit with Thai visitors in the cool season, who come for the evening walking street, cycling along the river and sunrise over a sea of mist from Phu Thok hill. Early morning alms giving is a gentle local ritual.

Songthaews leave town before 5:30 am for Phu Thok sunrise; ask your guesthouse the night before.

gems.what: A Lao-style temple with murals and an old ordination hall in the town centre.

gems.name: Phu Pa Po
gems.what: A cone-shaped hill nicknamed the Fuji of Loei, lovely at sunset.

localFavs.name: Khao poon
localFavs.what: Rice noodles in coconut or fish curry, often eaten for breakfast.

localFavs.name: Maphrao kaeo
localFavs.what: Shredded coconut sweets, the town's signature souvenir.

localFavs.name: Grilled Mekong fish
localFavs.what: With sticky rice at riverside restaurants.

crowd.quietest: Weekday mornings from March to October.
crowd.busiest: Saturday evening on the walking street from November to January.
crowd.note: A Thai cool-season favourite; rooms sell out on winter weekends.

places.name: Trang Islands
places.line: Quiet Andaman islands: Koh Kradan's sandbar, Koh Ngai's calm bay and the Emerald Cave.
places.about: Off the Trang coast, a cluster of small islands offers clear water and few crowds. Koh Kradan has a long white beach and coral right off the shore, Koh Ngai has gentle resorts and easy swimming, and Koh Mook has village life and Tham Morakot, the Emerald Cave, where you swim through a dark tunnel into a hidden lagoon. Island-hopping longtails link them all.
tips: Visit the Emerald Cave at low tide and early in the day, before the tour boats from Lanta; a head torch helps.
Many resorts close in the rainy season, from about May to October; check before booking.
Bring cash: ATMs are rare on the islands.

Four-island longtail snorkel tour, per person

places.timeOfDay: Emerald Cave before 10 am; Kradan's Sunset Beach in the late afternoon.

popular.name: Emerald Cave (Tham Morakot)
popular.what: Swim through an 80 metre tunnel into a sunlit lagoon inside Koh Mook.

popular.name: Koh Kradan main beach
popular.what: Fine sand and coral gardens just off the shore.

popular.name: Koh Ngai
popular.what: A calm bay with soft sand and easy snorkelling.

gems.name: Koh Mook village
gems.what: A Muslim fishing village with small cafes and the island's sunset beach on the far side.

gems.name: Koh Chueak and Koh Waen
gems.what: Small rocks with excellent soft coral, a stop on most snorkel tours.

localFavs.name: Massaman curry
localFavs.what: A southern favourite at family restaurants on Koh Mook.

localFavs.name: Trang roast pork
localFavs.what: Crispy roast pork with dim sum, a Trang town breakfast.

localFavs.name: Grilled fish
localFavs.what: Fresh catch at beach shacks in the evening.

crowd.quietest: Early November and late April, at the edges of the season.
crowd.busiest: Christmas to New Year and February, when Emerald Cave queues form at midday.
crowd.note: Many resorts and boats stop from about May to October; seas can be rough.

places.name: Koh Phayam
places.line: A barefoot island with no cars, cashew orchards and long empty beaches.
places.about: Koh Phayam sits off Ranong near the Myanmar border, a short boat ride from the mainland. There are no cars, just narrow concrete paths through cashew and rubber trees to wide beaches with simple bungalows and reggae bars. It suits those who want hammocks, sunsets and hornbills more than nightlife.
tips: Book boats and rooms ahead in peak season; many places close from about May to October.
Rent a scooter to reach the beaches; paths are narrow and sandy, so ride slowly.
Bring enough cash; ATMs are few and can run dry.

fees.what: Speedboat Ranong to Koh Phayam, one way
Slow boat Ranong to Koh Phayam, one way

places.timeOfDay: Ao Yai for the long sunset walk; hornbills are easiest to spot early morning.

popular.name: Ao Yai (Long Beach)
popular.what: Three kilometres of sand with surfable waves in shoulder season and sunset bars.

popular.name: Ao Khao Kwai (Buffalo Bay)
popular.what: A pretty curved bay with rocks, swings and calm sunset views.

popular.name: Phayam village and pier
popular.what: The island's small hub of cafes, shops and the Thursday market.

gems.name: Ranong hot springs
gems.what: Raksawarin hot springs on the mainland, worth a stop before or after the boat.

gems.name: Koh Chang Ranong
gems.what: A tiny, even quieter neighbour with no roads, reached by longtail.

localFavs.name: Cashew nuts
localFavs.what: Grown on the island, sold roasted at village shops.

localFavs.name: Pad thai and curries
localFavs.what: At family-run bungalow kitchens.

localFavs.name: Fresh seafood barbecue
localFavs.what: Fish and prawns on beach grills in the evening.

crowd.quietest: November and April, when it is almost empty.
crowd.busiest: Christmas to February, still calm compared with Phuket.
crowd.note: Many bungalows and boats stop from about May to October.

places.name: Surin Islands
places.line: Remote marine park islands with some of Thailand's best snorkelling and a Moken village.
places.about: Mu Ko Surin lies 60 km off the Phang Nga coast, close to the Myanmar border. Shallow coral reefs ring the islands, and the water is very clear in the dry season. The islands are home to the Moken, a seafaring people; visits to their village are part of most trips and should be respectful.
tips: The park is open roughly mid-October to mid-May and closes in the monsoon.
Day trips from Khao Lak leave very early; overnight in park tents or bungalows to snorkel after the day boats leave.
Buy Moken handicrafts in the village rather than giving sweets or money to children.
places.best: Mid Oct to mid May (park open)

fees.what: Mu Ko Surin National Park (foreign adult)
Speedboat day trip from Khao Lak, with snorkel stops and lunch

places.timeOfDay: Day boats arrive around 10 am; overnight guests get the reefs to themselves early and late.

popular.name: Ao Mai Ngam
popular.what: A white-sand bay with the park campsite and good snorkelling.

popular.name: Ao Bon Moken village
popular.what: A village of Moken families on Surin Tai, visited with respect.

popular.name: Ao Chong Khad
popular.what: Park headquarters by a shallow channel with reef fish and turtles.

gems.name: Richelieu Rock
gems.what: A famous dive pinnacle near the park, known for whale sharks.

gems.name: Khura Buri
gems.what: The quiet mainland pier town; mangrove kayaking and a local night market.

localFavs.name: Park canteen meals
localFavs.what: Simple Thai dishes at the park headquarters.

localFavs.name: Khao Lak seafood
localFavs.what: Back on the mainland at Bang Niang night market.

crowd.quietest: Late October and early May, just after opening and before closing.
crowd.busiest: Christmas to February, when day boats arrive together late morning.
crowd.note: Closed about 15 May to 15 October each year.

places.name: Tarutao National Park
places.line: A wild, jungle-covered island park with long empty beaches, beyond busy Koh Lipe.
places.about: Tarutao National Park covers more than 50 islands near the Malaysian border. Koh Tarutao itself is big and forested, once a prison island, with long beaches, mangroves and a cliff-top viewpoint. Koh Adang, a short hop from Lipe, has jungle trails, waterfalls and views back over the turquoise bay.
tips: The park fee covers all its islands for a few days; keep the ticket if you have already paid on arrival at Lipe.
Tarutao's facilities are basic; stay at the park bungalows at Ao Pante and rent a bike.
Most of the park closes to overnight stays from about mid-May to mid-October.

places.timeOfDay: Koh Adang trails in the early morning; To-Bo cliff on Tarutao at sunset.
